name: Lemon juice / baking soda on scars
lead: Applying lemon juice, baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) or a paste of the two to scars is a do-it-yourself practice that circulates as a way to lighten and smooth marks left by acne, injuries or surgery. The idea, as practitioners describe it, is that lemon juice's acidity fades dark marks and that baking soda's grit exfoliates raised or rough skin, giving a more even complexion and a less visible scar.

No clinical studies of the practice itself were found. Reference material on related topics describes how scars are classified and treated in clinics, what citrus juice can do to skin in sunlight, and how popular home remedies built on baking soda and lemon juice have been characterized in the medical literature.[1][2][3][4]

The most documented risk is phytophotodermatitis, a reaction in which plant compounds called furanocoumarins on the skin react to UVA light, producing redness, burning and blisters, usually followed by dark pigmented marks that can last for years.[2][3]

chain: Acidic juice and an abrasive powder applied to a scar
Scar blends in more with surrounding skin
angle.text: Practitioners apply the ingredients to lighten dark scar marks and to roughly smooth the skin surface so that a scar is less noticeable. The aim is a more even skin tone, achieved with inexpensive kitchen ingredients.

paras: The practice uses common kitchen ingredients. Lemon juice is acidic, and sodium bicarbonate is mildly alkaline in solution and has mild abrasive properties.[5] Variants include juice alone, baking soda mixed with water, or both combined into a paste that is left on the skin for a period and rinsed off.

Scars take several forms. Hypertrophic and keloid scars are raised, atrophic scars (common after acne or chickenpox) are sunken, and many scars also carry a color change.[1] The home remedy is usually discussed in connection with the color and surface texture of such marks.

Scar tissue forms when fibroblasts lay down densely packed, aligned collagen during repair, and Wikipedia notes that sweat glands and hair follicles do not regrow in it.[1] Hypertrophic scars look red and raised on lighter skin and dark brown on darker skin, which is why colour-lightening is a common goal of home remedies.[1] Keloids can grow beyond the original wound, are most common in darker-skinned people, and Wikipedia says surgical removal can worsen them.[1]
Home-remedy lists often present lemon juice as a natural bleaching agent and baking soda as a gentle scrub; the wiki records these as the claims proponents make rather than established effects.[5]

For comparison, the Wikipedia scar article lists silicone products, lasers (ablative lasers such as CO2 and Er:YAG are described as giving the best results for atrophic and acne scars, with longer healing and higher risk), corticosteroid injections for keloid and hypertrophic scars, and massage, with a weak evidence base reported for several of these. A Cochrane review it cites found weak evidence for silicone gel sheeting, based on poor-quality studies.[1] It also notes that some forms of vitamin C may fade dark pigment associated with scars, and that vitamin E and onion extract products have been found ineffective in research, with vitamin E causing contact dermatitis in up to a third of users.[1] The article reports that topical steroids are ineffective for keloids and that surgical excision alone recurs at close to 45 percent.[1] Dermatologists generally address dark post-inflammatory marks with sun protection and clinic-supervised pigment treatments.

Phytophotodermatitis follows contact with furanocoumarins, found in limes and other plants, and then UVA exposure. Reactions begin within about 24 to 48 hours and heal over several weeks, and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation typically remains, in some cases for several years and often more intensely in skin of colour.[2][3] DermNet describes lime as the best-known citrus trigger and does not mention lemon specifically; Wikipedia lists citrus including lime among triggers.[2][3] Dermatology guidance for the reaction includes cool compresses, avoiding the plant and using high-UVA sun protection.[3]

Sodium bicarbonate is listed as causing serious eye irritation.[5] A 2021 narrative review in Biochemical Pharmacology noted that claims that baking soda, lemon juice and apple cider vinegar are cures for a wide range of conditions circulate widely online, while describing acid-base therapies with established uses in specific medical conditions.[4]

DermNet lists the typical presentation as redness and often blistering about 24 to 48 hours after sun exposure, followed by ulceration or scaling in some cases, with patterns such as drip-shaped marks from lime juice, and notes that the reaction is a direct toxic effect rather than an allergy.[3] Management described includes cool compresses, topical antiseptics, topical steroids and analgesia, and starting a high-UVA sunscreen and covering the skin as soon as exposure is recognised may reduce severity.[3] This matters for scars because a new dark patch can sit on top of the mark the person hoped to lighten.

Acidity is also a concern for teeth: laboratory and in-situ studies use lemon juice (pH 2.5, about 4.25 percent citric acid) as a severe erosive challenge to enamel, illustrating that undiluted lemon juice is strongly acidic.[6][7] Those studies concern enamel, not skin.

The practice belongs to a wider tradition of kitchen-ingredient skin care, including lemon juice for dark spots and baking soda scrubs for rough skin. A 2021 narrative review in Biochemical Pharmacology notes that claims that baking soda, lemon juice and apple cider vinegar cure conditions from cancer to COVID-19 circulate widely online, while describing acid-base therapies with established uses in constipation, epilepsy, metabolic acidosis and peptic ulcers.[4] A 2014 T Nation post jokes about soaking the face in mineral water plus lemon juice and rubbing it with banana peel, an example of the home-remedy skincare banter that appears on bodybuilding forums.[8]

No studies found. Clinical trials that involve lemon juice concern drug interactions, kidney-stone prevention and dental erosion rather than scars; none tested lemon juice or baking soda on scars.[6][7][9]

lore.intro: Lemon juice and baking soda are mentioned occasionally as skin remedies in fitness and appearance forums, usually as quick jokes or passing tips rather than as an extended protocol.[8]

claims.claim: Lemon juice lightens scars and dark marks because it is acidic.
claims.believers: Proponents of home remedies say the acidity bleaches pigment so marks blend into the surrounding skin.[8]
claims.experts: No published study has tested lemon juice on scars; dermatology sources document that citrus plus sunlight can cause phytophotodermatitis, which leaves long-lasting pigmentation.[2][3]

claims.claim: Baking soda scrubs smooth raised or rough scars.
claims.believers: Users describe the powder as a cheap exfoliant that sands down texture over repeated use.[8]
claims.experts: No studies of baking soda for scars were found; clinical options such as silicone, lasers and steroid injection have their own, mostly modest, evidence bases.[1]

card.summary: Kitchen-ingredient scar remedy; no studies found, and citrus juice is a known cause of light-triggered skin reactions.
card.aka: DIY scar exfoliation, lemon and bicarbonate paste
card.note: Citrus juice plus sunlight can cause blistering and long-lasting dark marks (phytophotodermatitis).

quick.overview:
This home remedy involves rubbing lemon juice, baking soda (sodium bicarbonate), or a mix of the two on scars, with the idea of lightening or exfoliating them.
No studies were found testing this practice for scars. Separate reference material documents that citrus juice can cause skin reactions with sunlight.
quick.mechanism: Believers' reasoning typically centres on lemon juice's acidity as a lightener and baking soda's abrasiveness as an exfoliant. This reasoning is not supported by published trials.
quick.risks: Wikipedia describes phytophotodermatitis, a reaction that follows contact with plant furanocoumarins (found in citrus such as lime) and UV-A light, producing redness, burning and blisters within about 48 hours, and pigment marks that can persist for years. Sodium bicarbonate is listed as causing serious eye irritation.
